title: Scepter POC — dedicated capacity & autoscale lab notes
content:
Context:
This doc captures our lab experiments and early recommendations for the Scepter customer POC: sizing a Dedicated GPU pool, validating autoscaling policies, and producing a first-order GPU cost estimate. The customer workload is an interactive chat endpoint (multi-turn), heavy use of function/tool calling, and occasional long-response batch jobs (summaries). Objective is to hit a 200ms P95 latency SLO for short-turn requests, keep monthly committed spend within target, and provide transparent fallback behavior to Hosted if capacity is constrained.

High-level requirements (from sales + SE discovery):
- Peak concurrent interactive sessions: ~40 sessions (concurrent open connections executing generation)
- 95th percentile request length: 80 tokens in, 120 tokens out (short), long jobs up to 2,500 output tokens but low frequency (~1% of requests)
- Expected steady-state traffic: 6 RPS average; peak burst up to 40 RPS during feature launches or marketing events
- Latency SLO for interactive: P95 <= 200ms (short requests), P99 <= 500ms
- Budget target for committed monthly spend: $35k (GPU + infra) with ability to burst to pay-as-you-go for spikes

Key constraints we tested in lab:
1) Hardware options: A100-40GB (on-prem equivalent), H100-80GB (cloud), and mixed pool strategies.
2) Model family: Scepter is validating LLaMA-2-13B and a distilled 7B variant for low-latency paths. 13B used for high-quality outputs and long jobs.
3) Quantization: 4-bit int8/4 variants produced ~1.5-1.8x speedups; quality regressions acceptable for short-turn variants only.

Experiment summary (testbed config):
- Load generator: vegeta-based script with realistic think times, session stickiness, and occasional long-job injection (1% probability). Config available in linked PR.
- Serving runtime: dedicated pool simulated using 2x H100 nodes (80GB) and 4x A100 nodes for mixed pool tests. Each node running Redwood runtime with continuous batching enabled, dynamic KV cache pinned per-session.
- Batch tuning: batch windows 5ms/10ms/25ms were evaluated. Default recommendation: 10ms window for interactive to balance latency/throughput.

Observations and measurements:
- Single H100 node (80GB) with model-quantization=Q4 and batch-window=10ms: sustainable interactive throughput ~60 short requests/sec (120 output tokens avg) while keeping P95 latency ~170ms.
- A100 nodes showed ~0.85x relative throughput vs H100 for 13B with same quantization and batching. For cost-limited customers, A100 is acceptable for baseline but requires additional nodes for equivalent headroom.
- KV cache hit-rate significantly affects long session latency: with session affinity enabled and cache pinning, we observed 20-30% token-cost reduction and 15% latency improvement.
- Long jobs (2.5k tokens) monopolize a GPU for the duration. Strategies to mitigate: dedicated long-job worker queue (preemptible/spot instances), or model-slicing where long jobs are scheduled on A100-only nodes with relaxed latency SLO.

Autoscale policy prototypes (what we tried):
Policy A — Utilization-driven (simple):
- Scale up when average GPU utilization > 70% for 60s. Add 1 node.
- Scale down when average GPU utilization < 35% for 300s. Remove 1 node.
Pros: straightforward. Cons: reactive to bursts; slow to react to sudden spikes.

Policy B — Hybrid buffer + predictive (recommended):
- Maintain committed pool sized for 95% of expected baseline traffic (see sizing calc below).
- Keep a small hot spare buffer (10% headroom) always online for short bursts.
- Predictive scaler uses short-timeseries linear regression on RPS (30s window) — proactively spins up additional nodes when predicted RPS > threshold for next 60s.
- Use pre-warmed standing-burst nodes (prewarmed replicas) that accept traffic within 5-12s of scale decision instead of cold GCE provisioning.
- Fallback chain: if dedicated pool saturates and predictive scale cannot provision within Xs, route overflow traffic to Hosted tier (fallback model variant: distilled 7B) with degraded quality but preserved latency.
Pros: balances cost and latency during short bursts. Cons: more complex and requires prewarm management.

Policy C — Token-budget throttling + graceful degradation:
- Enforce per-customer token budget for long jobs; if long-job queue length > 5, throttle or schedule to off-peak windows.
- Introduce adaptive admission control for new interactive sessions if P95 > 250ms, either queue or route to hosted.

Sizing calculation (first-order) — baseline commitment recommendation:
Assumptions: 6 RPS steady, 40 concurrent sessions, avg request tokens in+out 200, 95% short requests, 1% long jobs. Using H100 numbers from lab: one H100 handles ~60 short requests/sec under Q4 with batch-window 10ms.
- Baseline demand headroom: we size for 6 RPS + 20% buffer = 7.2 RPS -> one H100 sufficient for baseline short workload.
- Peak sizing (40 RPS burst): 40 / 60 = 0.667 H100-equivalent per 60 short requests/sec metric? This is misleading: bursts are concurrent, not sustained. For 40 RPS sustained short requests, need 1 H100 (taking into account parallelism), but long-job contention changes things.
- Long-job mitigation: allocate 0.5 H100-equivalent capacity reserved for long jobs (or route them to a separate long-job pool).
Recommendation: Commit to 1 x H100 dedicated + 1 x A100 reserved as warm standby (mixed pool). Have autoscale policy B to spin additional H100 nodes when predictive scaler signals.

Cost estimate (first-order monthly committed cost) — rough numbers we used in lab
- H100 equivalent hourly cost (committed): $19/hr (example committed rate) -> monthly (720 hrs) = $13,680 per H100
- A100 equivalent hourly cost (committed): $10/hr -> monthly = $7,200 per A100
- Baseline commit recommendation: 1 H100 + 1 A100 = $20,880/mo (GPU only).
- Add overheads (networking, system nodes, storage, support margin ~25%) => target committed spend ~ $26k/mo. Leaves room for burst allowance to hit customer's $35k target using pay-as-you-go extra nodes for spikes.
Notes: these numbers are placeholders and should be replaced with final quotes from finance/partnerships. They are consistent with the relative H100 vs A100 delta we saw in our cloud region testbed.

Operational playbook highlights:
- Warm start strategy: keep a small number of prewarmed replicas per node type. Prewarmed replicas are process-level warm kernels with model loaded but not serving traffic; they respond inside 3s to accept traffic.
- Eviction policy: if memory fragmenting or high OOM frequency observed, prefer to gracefully drain older sessions to Hosted rather than kill active ones.
- Rollout recommendations: Canary 10% canary traffic on Dedicated pool after deploy; measure P95/P99 and token-cost before 100% rollout.
- Monitoring: instrument token-level cost, per-route latency, cache hit-rate, and per-node queue length. Set alerts at P95>200ms or queue length > 25 per node.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Long jobs saturate GPUs causing interactive latency regressions. Mitigation: long-job queue and separate worker pool or preemptible nodes; admission control when queue length high.
- Risk: Predictive scaler false positives cause wasted commit. Mitigation: short holdback windows and use prewarmed replicas rather than full node provisioning where possible.
- Risk: Quantization causes subtle quality regressions. Mitigation: route a fraction (5%) of interactive traffic to non-quantized path for continual quality checks; integrate Redwood Optimize evals to watch for regressions.

Experiment log (selected entries):
- 2025-08-14: Baseline H100 single-node run with 10ms batching; observed unstable P99 under long-job injection. Logged in SVC-2468.
- 2025-08-20: Mixed-pool (1 H100 + 2 A100) test with prewarm warm-replica strategy; improved spike handling, P95 stayed under 190ms for 95% of runs.
- 2025-08-28: Predictive scaler prototype tested; we observed 70% reduction in time-to-scale (compared to naive policy) for 30s bursts.

Open action items / next steps:
- Get committed pricing guidance from partnerships/pricing (Finance) and update final cost table (owner: Evan Holt, due 2025-09-10).
- Wire up the predictive scaler prototype to the customer's telemetry feed for a 2-week observation window (owner: Marta Silva, due 2025-09-17).
- Implement long-job queue with separate worker pool in staging and test with real customer long-job samples (owner: Jin Park, due 2025-09-24).
- Create a short customer-facing appendix that maps these technical recommendations to contract commit tiers and expected SLA behavior during bursts (owner: Priya Raman, due 2025-09-07).

Appendix: Load generator snippet (vegeta-like pseudoconfig)
- sessions: 200
- think_time_distribution: exp(mean=2s)
- long_job_injection: rate=0.01, output_tokens=2500
- request_profile: 95% short(path="/v1/chat", tokens_in=80, tokens_out=120), 5% system-ops

Notes to self: keep this doc focused on lab evidence + clear recommended commit. Save spreadsheets into Confluence and reference in customer appendix rather than embedding raw CSV here.

End of doc.
